## 9. What changed since the last chronicles (v2), and what is still to come

This chronicle (v3, seed 1) ran on the build of 2026-11-11 evening. Use it to see how the *politics* behaves. The economy still fails over a century (see "Known problems in this build"), so read the colony's material history as a struggling colony, not a balanced one.

### Changed since v2

**Who votes and why**
- **The population blocks are the voters.** Opinions, loyalties and grievances live on the people (grouped by area, income band, occupation, employment status and philosophy) and travel with them when they change jobs, income or home.
  - Who may vote comes from the electoral law: voting age, residency and non-citizen rules, with a 6-month lead before elections.
  - Turnout is about 80% (the old voter groups gave about 93%).
- **Eight philosophies** (labour, market, environment, equality, liberty, stability, development, institutions). Each colony draws its own variants and mix, and every occupation contains several philosophies.
- **A new political axis: loyal to the home world ↔ independence**, and a new concern, the colonial burden. Colony-born generations drift toward independence.

**Elections and campaigns (new: Ella)**
- A Swedish-style election year:
  - themes chosen 12 months out;
  - an Almedalen-style politics week;
  - a short campaign with election huts, posters and targeted ads;
  - leaders' debates with gaffes and momentum, and a final debate.
- **Attack ads** that can backfire, **opposition research** that can uncover real secrets (through the legal scandal path), **smears** that can lead to defamation cases, and tactical **support votes** for allies near the 4% threshold.

**Parliament and government**
- **Bills:**
  - governing parties only propose what they will all vote for;
  - a defeated change is not resubmitted to the same parliament;
  - a government cannot flip-flop on its own change within 3 years.
- **Coalitions:**
  - confidence-and-supply deals ask only for achievable things;
  - no-confidence motions happen when a government lacks a majority and an alternative exists.
- **Issue credibility:** a governing party that fails on its signature issue loses credibility on it.
- **Turnout recalibrated**, and donations spread across parties.
- **AI governments decide what the state builds,** by their politics. No hidden autopilot; nothing is built behind a human government's back.
- **States of emergency:** governments declare them in serious crises, and parliament approves and renews them. Measures: export ban, price controls, rationing.
- **District maps:** drawn by law, with constitutional limits, a fix for unbalanced maps, and gerrymandering by governments with little regard for institutional norms. Inactive until settlements exist as areas; see below.

**The home world and the colony**
- The home world is an actor with need, patience, its view of the colony's loyalty, and legitimacy. On each ship (every 18–30 months, irregular) it inspects, sanctions, answers petitions and may raise its demands.
- **Colony politics:** petitions, refusing the quota, and independence (101 seats plus a referendum). The home world can respond with recognition, autonomy or a punitive expedition.

**Economy (Bob)**
- **No home-world lifeline.** A founding endowment instead; ships bring migrants.
- **Firms pay out surplus cash** (no more hoarding).
- **Debt restructuring** after a default.
- **Rents fall** when people can't pay.
- **Plants are repaired:** by maintenance, by repair crews even without parts, and by a cold start after blackouts.
- **Companies build new plants themselves.** The public utility plans ahead with a 15% safety margin on power, water, materials and parts.
- **Plants that can't be repaired are sold:** to another company, the workers, or the state.
- **Supply chains:** firms supply themselves from their own stock and move inputs between their sites; materials go first to strategic expansions.
- **Licences are renewed** (this was part of the old Year-11 collapse).
- **Real company names**, and a fixed real-income indicator.

**Law (Anni)**
- **Crisis law:** violations, inquiries, prosecutions, compensation and emergency powers.
- **The colonial charter:** quota, smuggling, home-world sanctions, independence procedures.
- **Districting and land law:** titles, sale and lease policy, rent control, eviction rules.

**Readability**
- This chronicle shows what became of each bill (in force, rejected or cancelled), the confidence-and-supply deals, and a campaign section per election.

### What this run shows
- **The independence movement emerges by itself:** Independence Party, Free Colony Movement, Sovereign Colony League and Self-Determination Party rise from about Year 68 and lead governments, as colony-born generations drift away from the home world.
- **No-confidence votes now bring down governments** (6 times), where before they never did.
- **Laws keep changing all century:** 448 changes, 0 legal rejections, 17 defeated bills.

### Known problems in this build
- **Runaway landslides (a bug, under investigation).** The Founders' Party jumped from 8% to 70% (Year 28 → 32). Late in the century single parties took 94% and 93% of the vote, holding every seat in parliament. Real democracies don't produce this; a feedback loop in the vote model is suspected.
- **The real-income figure explodes again late in the run** (millions). It's a reporting bug, not real wealth; Bob has been told.
- **The economy still fails over a century.** In Bob's 6-colony test every colony has a famine between Year 10 and 38, and food then stays 40–68% short. The colony no longer dies outright: repair crews bring power back. Bob is tracing why farms don't recover.
- **A suspected runaway landslide:** in one test colony the Founders' Party gained about 94 points in a single election year. Under investigation.

### Still to come (the next full set of three chronicles, after the economy passes)
- **Fabrication kits** (your proposal): a crude parts workshop and smelter at landing, upgradeable Mk I → III.
- **Governments securing the essentials** (your proposal): state farms, or investment incentives for companies, by ideology.
- **Areas on the terrain map:** the colony starts as Landing plus two outposts; settlements found, grow and split (rich enclaves, slums); districts drawn by law.
- **Housing and land:** housing decays on an S-curve, so old stock becomes cheap housing or slums; quality tiers; the state owns all land at founding and sells or leases it.
- **Colonial goods:** a rare mineral and a native crop, shipped as the home world's quota at a charter price.
- **Random crises and company greed:** droughts, epidemics, accidents and breakdowns, lost ships, speculative food crises, crashes. Greedy firms that skip safety or dump waste make them likelier. Hidden causes come out in inquiries.
- **Planet climate** (Terra): seasons, rain, storms, pollution drift, alien phenomena and barely-noticeable warming, feeding the hazards.
- **The 3D globe** is in the game, but it doesn't affect this text chronicle.
